segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they were approaching Jerusalem, at Bethphage and Bethany near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it you will find a colt tied up, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord needs it, and he will send it back here right away.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went off and found a colt tied at a door, outside on the street, and they untied it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of those standing there said to them,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “What are you doing, untying the colt?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They told them just as Jesus had said, and they let them go.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks over it, and he sat on it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Many spread their cloaks on the road, and others leafy branches they had cut from the fields.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest heaven!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. After looking around at everything, since the hour was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day, when they had left Bethany, he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see whether he might find anything on it. When he came to it he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He responded by saying to it,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his disciples were listening.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Jerusalem. He entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling and buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who sold doves,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he would not let anyone carry anything through the temple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching and saying to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is it not written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests and the scribes heard of it and began looking for a way to destroy him; for they were afraid of him, because the whole crowd was astonished at his teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And whenever evening came, they would go out of the city.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they passed by early in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter remembered and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has withered.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have faith in God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in their heart but believes that what they say is happening, it will be done for them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this reason I tell you, whatever you pray and ask for, believe that you have received it, and it will be done for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “By what authority are you doing these things? Or who gave you this authority to do these things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I will ask you one question. Answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The baptism of John: was it from heaven or from people? Answer me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They argued it out among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “What are we to say? If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: But are we to say, ‘From people’?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were afraid of the crowd, for everyone held that John really was a prophet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they answered Jesus,

segments.speaker: crowd
segments.text: “We do not know.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.”

notes.note: The Greek word means the young of a horse or a donkey. Mark does not say which, but a donkey is almost certainly meant: Matthew and John say so, and the scene recalls Zechariah 9:9, where Jerusalem's king arrives on a donkey's colt. An animal never yet ridden was thought fitting for sacred or royal use.

The Greek word can mean 'the Lord', 'the master' or 'the owner', and the phrase could be read 'its owner needs it'. Most translations take it as Jesus referring to himself as the Lord, as here. Some scholars think the wording is deliberately open, since bystanders would have heard only that someone with a claim on the animal required it.

The crowd's words come from Psalm 118:25–26, a psalm sung by pilgrims at the great festivals. 'Hosanna' represents a Hebrew plea meaning 'save, please'. By this period it seems also to have been used as a shout of acclamation, which is how it works here.

notes.phrase: it was not the season for figs
notes.note: Mark's remark makes the incident deliberately puzzling as a story about hunger alone. He places the fig tree on either side of the action in the temple, and most interpreters read the two together: the tree with leaves but no fruit is an acted sign of judgment on the temple. The prophets used the barren fig tree as an image for Israel (for example Jeremiah 8:13).

The word covers the whole temple complex, not only the sanctuary building. The trading took place in its large outer court, the one area open to non-Jews. Money changers exchanged everyday coinage for the currency accepted for the temple tax, and doves were the sacrifice prescribed for those who could not afford a larger animal.

Jesus joins Isaiah 56:7, on the temple as a house of prayer for all nations, to Jeremiah 7:11. The Greek word means a violent robber or bandit, not a petty thief or a cheat. In Jeremiah the 'den' is the hideout where robbers feel safe after their crimes, so the charge is that the temple is treated as a refuge by people who do wrong elsewhere, and not only that the trading there was dishonest.

notes.phrase: whenever evening came, they would go out
notes.traditional: when evening came, they went out
notes.note: The Greek construction can describe a repeated habit during these days in Jerusalem, as rendered here, or a single evening ('when evening came, they went out'), and translations are divided. Some manuscripts also read 'he would go out' in place of 'they'.
The Greek is literally 'have faith of God'. Almost all interpreters take this as faith directed toward God, as translated. A minority reads it as a reference to God's own faithfulness.

notes.phrase: believe that you have received it
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have a past tense, 'you received'. Many later manuscripts read 'you are receiving' or 'you will receive', which look like attempts to ease the surprising statement that the thing asked for should be regarded as already given. The past tense is followed here, as in most modern editions.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God's dwelling that a first-century hearer would have recognised. Most English translations flatten it to 'in heaven'. The plural is kept here because the Greek has it.

The word means a wrong done against God or another person. 'Trespasses' is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it mainly suggests entering someone's property unlawfully. Some translations simply use 'sins', which blurs the distinction from the more common Greek word for sin.

notes.phrase: so that your Father in the heavens may also forgive you your offenses.”
notes.note: The numbering passes from verse 25 to verse 27. Verse 26 ('But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in the heavens forgive your offenses') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and was probably added by copyists from Matthew 6:15. The Greek text translated here does not include it.

'Heaven' is here a reverent Jewish way of saying 'God' without using the name. The question is whether John acted on God's commission or only on human initiative. The same answer would apply to Jesus's own authority.
